links.outcome: False alarm burden and positive predictive value of fall-risk alerts
links.effect: Window-level high-risk PPV 6.25% (5/80); deployment false positive rate 8.2% (134 false alarms/1,634 alerts); deployment alert PPV 87.8% after episode-level aggregation; sensitivity 89.5% (51/57 episodes).
links.quote: We stress, however, that the extreme class imbalance (fall windows constitute only 0.05% of total windows, with a high-risk PPV of merely 6.25%) severely limits the stability and interpretability of sensitivity estimates; a single misclassification among the six fall events shifts sensitivity by roughly 17% points.

links.outcome: Overall accuracy masking poor high-risk classification under extreme class imbalance
links.effect: Reported accuracy was 94.2%, versus 97.98% for always-low-risk predictions. High-risk PPV was 6.25%; sensitivity was 83.3% (5/6), with one misclassification shifting sensitivity by approximately 17% points.
links.quote: A classifier that predicted “low risk” for every window would achieve 97.98% accuracy, which is actually higher than our model’s overall figure—the difference being that our model trades some majority-class accuracy for improved sensitivity to minority-class events, as intended by the focal loss objective.

links.outcome: Missed high-risk episodes and unnecessary alerts during field deployment
links.effect: Deployment sensitivity was 89.5% (51/57 high-risk episodes detected); reported false positive rate was 8.2% (134 false alarms/1,634 alerts). Separately reported active-alert PPV was 87.8%, using aggregated alert episodes.
links.quote: An important methodological note concerns the apparent discrepancy between the window-level high-risk PPV of 6.25% (Table 5 ) and the deployment-level total active-alert PPV of 87.8%: the former evaluates each individual 2-second window independently, whereas the latter evaluates temporally aggregated alert episodes that have passed through the rule-based warning engine’s trend filtering, contextual modifiers, and minimum-duration thresholds.

links.outcome: Fall incidence with active warnings versus passive monitoring
links.effect: Falls/person-month: 0.82 ± 0.35 versus 2.14 ± 0.61; RR = 0.38 (95% CI: 0.24–0.62). Non-randomized, bundled intervention; exploratory association rather than causal efficacy evidence.
links.quote: During a three-month field deployment involving 80 participants, the group receiving active alerts recorded 62% fewer falls than the passive-monitoring control group, but we cannot attribute this outcome to the real-time warning mechanism alone given the non-randomized design and the additional intervention components (daily risk summaries, caregiver notifications) that could independently alter behavior; this finding is strictly exploratory.

links.outcome: User satisfaction, usability, and wearing adherence during the pilot
links.effect: User satisfaction averaged 4.3/5; wearing compliance reached 91.3% of waking hours. The System Usability Scale score was 82.5 ± 7.8.
links.quote: User satisfaction averaged 4.3/5 on a Likert scale, and wearing compliance reached 91.3% of waking hours.
